title: Creating New Forms of Expression

slides.text: For most of human history, words had to carry almost everything we wanted to communicate. We had no practical way to combine images, sound, movement, color, and timing as ordinary parts of a message.
Today, those limitations are largely gone. We can combine all of these forms of expression with extraordinary freedom.
Yet, the languages we use were shaped in a world where these possibilities did not exist.
We already have the ingredients. What we do not yet have is a developed language for using them together.
So what would happen if we began developing a language of expression designed for the possibilities we have now?
Words would still have a central place. But they would no longer have to carry everything alone.
Images, sound, movement, color, silence, and timing could also carry meaning as parts of the message.
Yet the deeper expressive power can go beyond the elements themselves as symbols.
Meaning can emerge from what happens to them through time—how they appear, move, react, combine, separate, change, or disappear, and how one moment gives way to the next.
In this way, much of the language can come from events, transformations, and relationships unfolding through time, rather than from the symbolic meaning of the elements alone.

When these possibilities work together, an image can carry one idea while its movement adds another, its timing changes how it is felt, sound alters its emotional meaning, and its transformation reveals something new.
Meaning emerges from the whole experience and from the relationships between its parts.
A repeated pulse can make something feel urgent.
Several elements moving toward the same point can express gathering or agreement.
A color spreading through an image can suggest a change in mood.
A sudden transition can make the next moment feel like an interruption or revelation.
Here, language does not mean replacing words.
It means developing reusable ways for images, sound, movement, color, silence, timing, and words to work together to express meaning.
But how do we actually write in this new language?
We can begin with something familiar: the digital slide. Here, a slide is simply the canvas for one moment in the sequence.
An effect changes what happens within a slide.
A transition shapes what happens between one slide and the next.
In this project, effects and transitions are some of the tools that make this kind of expression possible.
They can become reusable forms of expression—something like a growing visual vocabulary.
The goal of this project is to create a language of expression that grows as people use it.
Each new idea, creative solution, and discovery can add something to that language.
For this to happen, people need a practical way to create new parts of the language themselves.
This project is designed so that people do not need to be experienced programmers to create new components of the language.

Creating a custom effect may be much easier than it sounds.
There are two reasons for this.
First, modern AI systems can write and modify much of the code.
Second, because the project is open, the AI can examine the existing effects and understand how a new one needs to fit into the system.
In practice, a person opens the open-source project folder in an AI coding tool—for example, Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, or another tool that can work directly with a codebase.
They fill in a form describing what the new effect or transition should do.
They copy the prompt generated by the form and paste it into the AI chat.
The AI can then examine the existing project, create the necessary files, and fit the new effect or transition into the system.

Instead of beginning with the question,
“Do I know how to program this?”,
the creator can begin with a different question:
What do I want to express?

description: Exploring how images, sound, movement, color, timing, and words can grow into a shared language of expression.
